## One portfolio, twelve countries {.hook background-color="#FAF7F2"}

Over 1980–2007, a US investor holding only US stocks earned **1.11% a month**
with a standard deviation of **4.25**. The same investor, holding the optimal
international portfolio, earned **1.40%** with a standard deviation of **4.74**.

::: incremental
-   More return and more risk — so the comparison needs a measure that handles
    both at once.
-   Adjusted for risk, the international portfolio wins in **every one of the
    twelve countries** studied.
-   Today is about why that gain exists, how large it is, and what stops
    investors from taking it.
:::

::: notes
Open with the numbers rather than the theory, because the theory is easier to
accept once they have seen the size of the prize.

A US investor who held only American shares earned one point one one percent a
month. The same investor holding the best international mix earned one point
four zero.

*[ask]* Is that better?

Do not accept yes. The standard deviation also rose, from four twenty-five to
four seventy-four. More return and more risk is not obviously better, and that
is exactly why we need a measure that puts the two together - which is where
the Sharpe ratio comes in, in about ten minutes.

Then the second bullet, which is the one worth remembering: once you adjust for
risk, the international portfolio beat the domestic one in all twelve countries
in the study. Not most. All.

Last line sets up the session. Why does the gain exist, how big is it, and why
does almost nobody take it.
:::

# 1 · International portfolio investment {.divider .center background-color="#06302F"}

## 1 · Why diversification works

Portfolio risk falls as you add securities, but only because their returns do
not move together. **Correlation**, not the number of holdings, does the work.

Average correlation of monthly stock returns, **within** a country (on the
diagonal) and **between** countries:

| | AU | FR | DE | JP | NL | CH | UK | US |
|:---|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| **Australia** | **0.586** | | | | | | | |
| **France** | 0.286 | **0.576** | | | | | | |
| **Germany** | 0.183 | 0.312 | **0.653** | | | | | |
| **Japan** | 0.152 | 0.238 | 0.300 | **0.416** | | | | |
| **Netherlands** | 0.241 | 0.344 | 0.509 | 0.282 | **0.624** | | | |
| **Switzerland** | 0.358 | 0.368 | 0.475 | 0.281 | 0.517 | **0.664** | | |
| **United Kingdom** | 0.315 | 0.378 | 0.299 | 0.209 | 0.393 | 0.431 | **0.698** | |
| **United States** | 0.304 | 0.225 | 0.170 | 0.137 | 0.271 | 0.272 | 0.279 | **0.439** |

::: notes
Start from the mechanism, not the table.

Adding securities reduces risk only if they do not all move together. If every
stock in your portfolio rose and fell as one, holding fifty would be no safer
than holding one. So the thing that matters is correlation, and the number of
holdings only matters through it.

*[point at the diagonal]*

The bold figures are the correlation between two stocks picked inside the same
country. Everything below is the correlation between two different countries.

*[ask]* Compare the diagonal with the off-diagonal. What do you notice?

Every off-diagonal number is smaller. Two British stocks move together at
nought point seven; a British and a Japanese stock at nought point two.

That is the whole case for international diversification in one table. You
cannot escape the common factor inside one economy - the same interest rate,
the same recession, the same government. Across economies, you partly can.

One detail if they ask: the US row is low all the way across, and its own
diagonal is the lowest at nought point four four. A large, diverse economy
provides more internal diversification than a small one - which also means a US
investor has less to gain abroad than a Swiss investor does.
:::

## 1 · How far risk falls

```{r}
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.3
n <- 1:50
mk <- function(floor_, speed, lab) {
  data.frame(n = n, risk = floor_ + (1 - floor_) * exp(-(n - 1) / speed),
             market = lab)
}
lv <- c("Swiss stocks only", "U.S. stocks only", "International")
d <- rbind(mk(.44, 6, lv[1]), mk(.27, 8, lv[2]), mk(.12, 11, lv[3]))
d$market <- factor(d$market, levels = lv)
ends <- data.frame(n = 50, risk = c(.44, .27, .12),
                   market = factor(lv, levels = lv))

ggplot(d, aes(n, risk, colour = market)) +
  geom_hline(data = ends, aes(yintercept = risk, colour = market),
             linetype = "22", linewidth = .4) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(IF_COL$slate, IF_COL$clay, IF_COL$teal700)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(.12, .27, .44, 1),
                     labels = c("0.12", "0.27", "0.44", "1.00")) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1.02)) +
  labs(x = "Number of stocks in the portfolio", y = "Portfolio risk", colour = NULL,
       title = "Diversification stops working at a floor - and the floor is lower abroad",
       caption = "Schematic, following Solnik. Risk of a single stock set to 1.") +
  theme_if() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

Keep adding stocks and risk falls — but only to a floor. What remains is
**systematic risk**: the part no amount of diversification removes.

::: notes
Three curves, same shape, three different floors.

*[trace one curve with a finger]*

Each one starts at the risk of holding a single stock and falls as you add more.
Steeply at first - the second stock helps enormously - then barely at all. By
about twenty holdings you have captured most of what is available.

*[ask]* Why does it flatten instead of going to zero?

Because some risk is common to every company in the set. A recession, a rate
rise, a war. Diversification removes what is specific to one firm; it cannot
remove what hits all of them. That remainder is systematic risk.

*[point at the three dashed lines]*

Now the point of the slide. The floor is not the same height. A Swiss investor
diversifying only inside Switzerland stops at nought point four four. An
American stops at nought point two seven - a bigger, more varied economy. Go
international and the floor drops to nought point one two.

Say the consequence plainly: the gain from going abroad is largest for
investors in small economies. A Swiss investor has far more to gain than an
American one, which is a result you can predict from the correlation table we
just looked at.
:::

## 1 · Measuring performance

:::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
The **world beta** measures how sensitive a national market is to world market
movements — the systematic part, which diversification cannot remove.

The **Sharpe performance measure** puts return and risk in one number: excess
return per unit of total risk.

$$SHP_i = \frac{\bar R_i - R_f}{\sigma_i}$$

-   $\bar R_i$ — mean return of market $i$
-   $\sigma_i$ — standard deviation of those returns
-   $R_f$ — the risk-free rate (US Treasury bill)
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
Monthly, 1980–2007:

| Market | Mean | SD | β | SHP |
|:---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Sweden | 1.67 | 7.11 | 1.17 | **0.168** |
| Netherlands | 1.35 | 5.19 | 0.99 | **0.167** |
| United States | 1.11 | 4.25 | 0.88 | 0.149 |
| Hong Kong | 1.54 | 8.77 | 1.06 | 0.121 |
| France | 1.20 | 6.00 | 1.04 | 0.121 |
| Japan | 0.92 | 6.53 | 1.10 | **0.067** |
:::
::::

::: notes
Two measures, and they answer different questions.

Beta asks how much of a market's movement comes from the world moving. A beta
of one point one means that market amplifies world swings; below one, it damps
them.

The Sharpe ratio asks something more practical: how much extra return did you
get for each unit of risk you carried? Excess return on top, total risk
underneath.

*[point at the formula]*

Note what is in the denominator - total risk, the standard deviation, not beta.
That matters: Sharpe judges you on everything that moved, not only the part
correlated with the world.

*[point at the table]*

Now read it with them, because the ranking is not the ranking of returns.

*[ask]* Hong Kong returned one point five four a month and the United States
one point one one. Which was the better investment?

The United States, comfortably. Hong Kong's standard deviation was eight
seventy-seven against four twenty-five, so its Sharpe ratio is a third lower.
High returns bought with high volatility are not a free lunch - they are a
purchase.

And Japan at the bottom: the lowest mean return in the table, with high
volatility. Nineteen eighty to two thousand and seven covers the bubble and the
lost decade.
:::

## 1 · The optimal portfolio

Investors prefer more wealth to less and dislike risk. With a risk-free asset
available, the best portfolio of risky assets is the one that **maximises the
Sharpe ratio**:

$$\max (SHP_{op}) = \frac{\bar R_{op} - R_f}{\sigma_{op}}$$

:::: columns
::: {.column width="46%"}
With two risky assets A and B:

$$\bar R_{op} = x_A \bar R_A + x_B \bar R_B$$

$$\sigma_{op} = \left[x_A^2\sigma_A^2 + x_B^2\sigma_B^2 + 2x_Ax_B\sigma_{AB}\right]^{1/2}$$
:::

::: {.column width="54%"}
Substituting and maximising with respect to the weights gives

$$x_A = \frac{(\bar R_A - R_f)\sigma_B^2 - (\bar R_B - R_f)\sigma_{AB}}
{(\bar R_A - R_f)\sigma_B^2 + (\bar R_B - R_f)\sigma_A^2 - (\bar R_A - R_f + \bar R_B - R_f)\sigma_{AB}}$$

$$x_B = 1 - x_A$$
:::
::::

::: notes
Do not derive this. Explain what it is doing and then use it.

The investor can always put money in the risk-free asset, so the only question
left is which mix of risky assets to hold. The answer is the mix with the best
reward per unit of risk - the highest Sharpe ratio. That mix is the same for
everybody, regardless of how brave they are; how brave you are only decides how
much of your money goes into it rather than into Treasury bills.

*[left column]*

The portfolio return is just the weighted average of the two returns. The
portfolio risk is not - and the third term in that bracket is why. The
covariance term is what makes the whole thing work: if the two assets move
against each other, that term is negative and the portfolio is less risky than
either asset alone.

*[right column]*

This expression is what you get when you maximise the ratio with respect to the
weights. It looks unpleasant and it is only algebra. In the exam you substitute
numbers into it, which is what we are about to do.

*[ask]* Before we compute anything: look at the numerator. What makes the weight
on A large?

A high excess return on A, a high variance on B, and a low covariance between
them. All three say the same thing - hold more of the asset that contributes
return and less of the one that duplicates risk you already have.
:::

## 1 · Problem 5.1

::: ask
For 1980.1–2001.12, monthly, in percent, for the US and Netherlands indexes:

$\bar R_{US} = 1.26$, $\sigma^2_{US} = 19.62$ · $\bar R_{NL} = 1.38$,
$\sigma^2_{NL} = 26.52$ · $R_f = 0.55$ · $\sigma_{US,NL} = 14.14$

1.  What is the optimal international portfolio?
2.  What are its expected return and risk?
3.  What is its Sharpe performance?
4.  How does that compare with the US alone?
:::

::: notes
Ten minutes in pairs. Calculators out — this one is pure substitution, and it is
the kind of question that appears on the exam.

Two things to flag before they start, because both cost marks.

The data gives you **variances**, not standard deviations. Nineteen point six
two is a variance; the standard deviation is its square root, four point four
three.

And the covariance is given directly, fourteen point one four. They do not need
to build it from the correlation, although it is worth noting where it comes
from: four forty-three times five fifteen times nought point six two.

*[let them work, then take it on the board]*

Excess returns first: US nought point seven one, Netherlands nought point eight
three.

Numerator: nought seven one times twenty-six fifty-two, minus nought eight
three times fourteen fourteen. Seven point zero nine.

Denominator: thirteen point three four.

So x_US is fifty-three percent and the Netherlands forty-seven.

*[ask]* The Netherlands has the higher return. Why is it not the bigger half?

Because it also has the higher variance, and the two markets are correlated at
nought point six two, so the extra Dutch return does not buy much extra
diversification.

Then the portfolio: return one point three two, standard deviation four point
two nine, Sharpe nought point one seven nine.

And the comparison, which is the real answer to the question: the US alone had a
Sharpe of nought point one six zero. Both markets individually are below the
mix. That is diversification - the combination beats both of its parts, and
nothing about either market changed.

**Worked.** Excess returns 0.71 and 0.83. Numerator = 0.71 x 26.52 - 0.83 x
14.14 = 7.09. Denominator = 0.71 x 26.52 + 0.83 x 19.62 - 1.54 x 14.14 = 13.34.
x_US = 0.532, x_NL = 0.468. R_op = 1.316. Var = 18.40, SD = 4.29.
SHP_op = (1.316 - 0.55)/4.29 = 0.179, against SHP_US = 0.160 and SHP_NL = 0.161.
:::

## 1 · The efficient set, drawn

```{r}
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.6
mkt <- data.frame(
  code = c("AU","CN","FR","GM","HK","IT","JP","NL","SD","SW","UK","US"),
  mean = c(1.26,1.07,1.20,1.19,1.54,1.29,0.92,1.35,1.67,1.15,1.19,1.11),
  sd   = c(6.29,5.55,6.00,6.29,8.77,7.08,6.53,5.19,7.11,5.11,5.20,4.25))
rf  <- 0.55
oip <- data.frame(sd = 4.74, mean = 1.40)
slope <- (oip$mean - rf) / oip$sd

ggplot(mkt, aes(sd, mean)) +
  geom_abline(intercept = rf, slope = slope,
              colour = IF_COL$teal700, linewidth = .9) +
  geom_point(size = 2.4, colour = IF_COL$slate, shape = 4, stroke = 1.1) +
  geom_text(aes(label = code), vjust = -1, size = 3.4, colour = IF_COL$slate) +
  geom_point(data = oip, size = 3.6, colour = IF_COL$clay) +
  annotate("text", x = oip$sd, y = oip$mean + .13, label = "OIP",
           colour = IF_COL$clay, size = 4.4, fontface = "bold") +
  annotate("point", x = 0, y = rf, size = 2.6, colour = IF_COL$teal700) +
  annotate("text", x = .25, y = rf - .08, label = "risk-free 0.55",
           colour = IF_COL$teal700, size = 3.3, hjust = 0) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 9.5), ylim = c(0.4, 1.9)) +
  labs(x = "Standard deviation, % per month", y = "Mean return, % per month",
       title = "Twelve national markets, and the portfolio that beats all of them",
       caption = "Monthly returns 1980-2007. OIP for a US investor: 1.40% return, 4.74% risk.") +
  theme_if()
```

::: notes
This is the picture the algebra was building towards, so take a minute on it.

*[point at the crosses]*

Each cross is one national market: its average monthly return against its
standard deviation. Hong Kong far out on the right, high return and high risk.
The United States bottom left, modest return and the lowest risk of the twelve.

*[point at the OIP dot]*

The dot is the optimal international portfolio for a US investor. One point four
zero percent a month at a standard deviation of four point seven four.

*[ask]* Find a single country that is above and to the left of that dot.

There is none. Every individual market is worse - either less return for the
same risk, or more risk for the same return. A combination of twelve things is
better than any one of them.

*[trace the line from the risk-free point]*

The line starts at the risk-free rate and passes through the OIP. Its slope *is*
the Sharpe ratio, which is the cleanest way to see what that formula was doing:
of all the lines you could draw from the risk-free rate to some portfolio, the
optimal one is the steepest.

*[ask]* And what are the points on the line between the risk-free rate and the
dot?

Mixtures of Treasury bills and the optimal portfolio. Beyond the dot you are
borrowing at the risk-free rate to hold more of it. Which is why the mix is the
same for everyone and only the position along the line differs.
:::

## 1 · What the optimal portfolio holds

:::: columns
::: {.column width="46%"}
For a **US investor**, the optimal international portfolio over 1980–2007:

| Market | Weight |
|:---|--:|
| Netherlands | 31.11% |
| Sweden | 28.01% |
| United States | 20.70% |
| Hong Kong | 8.76% |
| Italy | 6.60% |
| Australia | 4.82% |
| **Total** | **100%** |
:::

::: {.column width="54%"}
Three things to notice:

-   Only **six** of the twelve markets appear at all. The others add nothing
    once these are held.
-   The investor's **own market is a fifth** of the portfolio, not the whole of
    it.
-   The weights are **not** proportional to market size. Sweden is a small
    market with a large weight, because its returns were high and only loosely
    correlated with the rest.

The composition differs by the investor's **domicile**, because each investor's
home market is already in their portfolio.
:::
::::

::: notes
*[cuttable - the composition matters less than the fact that a gain exists]*

Three things to draw out, and the third is the one that surprises people.

First, most markets get a weight of zero. The optimiser is not trying to own a
bit of everything - it drops any market whose risk and return are already
delivered by the ones it has kept.

Second, the US investor's own market is one fifth of the portfolio. Remember
that number, because at the end of the session we will see what investors
actually hold, and it is nothing like twenty percent.

Third, and this is worth pausing on.

*[ask]* Sweden is a small economy. Why is it twenty-eight percent of the
portfolio?

Not because it is big - weights here have nothing to do with market
capitalisation. Sweden had the highest Sharpe ratio in the table and its returns
were not closely tied to the others. High reward per unit of risk, and risk that
does not duplicate what you already carry.

Last line: the table on the original slide has a different column for each
investor's country, because a Dutch investor already holds Dutch assets in a way
an American does not. The optimal portfolio depends on where you start.
:::

## 1 · The size of the gain

```{r}
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.4
g <- data.frame(
  country = c("Japan","Canada","Italy","Germany","Australia","France",
              "Hong Kong","United Kingdom","United States","Switzerland",
              "Sweden","Netherlands"),
  dp  = c(.065,.081,.088,.109,.089,.103,.108,.112,.149,.152,.184,.160),
  oip = c(.177,.167,.152,.177,.152,.163,.171,.156,.194,.192,.215,.178))
g$country <- factor(g$country, levels = g$country[order(g$oip - g$dp)])

ggplot(g) +
  geom_segment(aes(y = country, yend = country, x = dp, xend = oip),
               colour = IF_COL$muted, linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(aes(y = country, x = dp), size = 2.8, colour = IF_COL$slate) +
  geom_point(aes(y = country, x = oip), size = 2.8, colour = IF_COL$clay) +
  annotate("text", x = .062, y = 12.4, label = "domestic only",
           colour = IF_COL$slate, size = 3.6, hjust = 0, fontface = "bold") +
  annotate("text", x = .205, y = 12.4, label = "optimal international",
           colour = IF_COL$clay, size = 3.6, hjust = 1, fontface = "bold") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(.05, .23), clip = "off") +
  labs(x = "Sharpe performance measure", y = NULL,
       title = "Every country gains - and the ones that gain most start furthest behind",

  theme_if() +

```

::: notes
One line per country. The grey dot is what that country's investors got holding
only their own market; the orange dot is the optimal international portfolio for
them. The gap is the gain.

*[ask]* Which country gains the most, and can anyone say why before I tell you?

Japan, by a long way - from nought point zero six five to nought point one seven
seven, nearly three times. Japanese investors spent this period in a market with
poor returns and high volatility, so almost anything else was an improvement.

*[point at the top of the chart]*

And the smallest gain is the Netherlands, which already had one of the best
domestic Sharpe ratios in the sample. The pattern is general: the worse your own
market, the more you gain by leaving it.

*[pause]*

Now the line that matters more than any individual country.

Every single bar points the same way. Twelve countries, twelve gains, no
exceptions. Whatever your starting point, the risk-adjusted performance improved
by going international.

*[ask]* So why is this not what everybody does?

Hold that - it is the last slide of the session.
:::

## 1 · The exchange rate comes with it

A US resident investing abroad earns the foreign return **and** whatever the
currency does:

$$R_{i\$} = R_i + e_i + R_i e_i \qquad \text{since} \qquad 1 + R_{i\$} = (1+R_i)(1+e_i)$$

where $R_i$ is the local-currency return and $e_i$ the change in the exchange
rate — positive when the foreign currency **appreciates** against the dollar.

::: keyidea
The currency affects **risk** through three separate channels:

$$Var(R_{i\$}) = Var(R_i) + Var(e_i) + 2\,Cov(R_i, e_i) + \Delta Var$$

its own volatility, its **covariance** with the local market, and the
cross-product term.
:::

::: notes
The point of this slide is that a foreign investment is two bets, not one, and
students routinely forget the second.

You buy Japanese shares. Two things then determine what you end up with: what
the shares do in yen, and what the yen does against your currency.

*[point at the formula]*

The multiplicative version on the right is the honest one - one plus the dollar
return equals one plus the local return, times one plus the currency change.
Expand it and you get the three terms on the left, of which the last is small
and the one people drop.

*[ask]* If the exchange rate adds a second source of randomness, does foreign
investing have to be riskier?

Not necessarily, and the key idea explains why. Look at the covariance term. If
the currency tends to rise when the local market falls, that covariance is
negative and the currency is partly cancelling the market - the two risks offset
rather than add.

So currency risk is not automatically bad news. It is an extra term that can
have either sign, and which sign it has is an empirical question for each
market.

Worth adding: this is also why the bond slide later says exchange risk makes
international bond diversification hard. In a bond portfolio the local return is
small and steady, so the currency term dominates everything.
:::

## 1 · Problem 5.2

::: ask
A US resident has just sold shares in a British firm. The shares returned
**15%** in pounds, over a period in which the pound **depreciated 5%** against
the dollar.

What is the dollar return, in percentage terms?
:::

::: notes
Two minutes. It is a one-line calculation and the point is the third term.

*[ask]* First, without computing: will the dollar return be above or below
fifteen percent?

Below. The pound fell, so each pound you bring home buys fewer dollars.

*[ask]* And is it exactly ten percent?

That is the trap, and most of the room will say yes. Fifteen minus five is ten,
and ten is wrong.

*[do it on the board]*

One plus fifteen percent, times one minus five percent. One point one five times
nought point nine five is one point zero nine two five. So nine point two five
percent.

Or in the additive form: fifteen, minus five, minus nought point seven five. That
last term is the cross-product - the currency loss applies to your investment
gains as well as to your original stake.

*[pause]*

Three quarters of a percent sounds trivial. Make the numbers bigger and it is
not: a fifty percent return with a thirty percent currency fall loses you fifteen
points to the cross term alone.

**Worked.** R$ = (1.15)(0.95) - 1 = 9.25%. Additive: 0.15 - 0.05 + (0.15)(-0.05)
= 0.15 - 0.05 - 0.0075 = 9.25%.
:::

## 1 · Other ways to get there

:::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**International bonds.** Less studied than equities, and exchange risk makes the
gains hard to realise — though **currency forwards** can hedge most of it away.

**International mutual funds.** Diversification bought at home: no extra
transaction or information costs, no legal barriers, and professional managers.

**Country funds.** Invest in a single foreign market — useful for building your
own allocation, or for reaching markets otherwise closed.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**ADRs.** Foreign shares repackaged to trade on a US exchange, in dollars.

**ETFs.** Track a foreign index and trade like a single stock.

**Hedge funds.** Privately pooled, aggressive and flexible — leverage, short
positions, derivatives, across currencies, bonds, stocks, commodities and
property. Sought for **absolute** returns, whether markets rise or fall, with
the risk that entails.
:::
::::

::: notes
*[cuttable - name international mutual funds in one line and move on]*

Do not read six boxes aloud. Group them and make one point.

Everything here is a different route to the same destination: foreign exposure
without personally opening a brokerage account in Tokyo.

*[left column, briefly]*

Bonds first, and note the honest caveat - with bonds the currency term swamps
the return term, so the diversification gain is harder to collect unless you
hedge it with the forwards from last session.

Then funds, which are the practical answer for almost everybody: one purchase,
at home, in your own currency.

*[right column]*

ADRs they have already met, in the stock market section. ETFs are the modern
version of the same idea - buy an index as if it were one share.

Hedge funds are the odd one out and worth flagging as such. The others buy
diversification. Hedge funds promise absolute return, which is a different
product with a different risk, and we come back to them next session.

*[ask]* If international mutual funds make this so easy, what is left of the
excuse for not diversifying?

Nothing - which is exactly the puzzle of the next slide.
:::

## 1 · Problem 5.3

::: ask
US-based international mutual funds, against the S&P 500 and the US MNC index,
monthly over 1977–1986:

| | Mean return | SD | $\beta_{US}$ |
|:---|--:|--:|--:|
| US-based international mutual funds | 1.58 | 5.78 | 0.69 |
| S&P 500 | 1.17 | 4.25 | 1.00 |
| US MNC index | 1.34 | 4.38 | 0.98 |

What is your analysis of their relative performance?
:::

::: {.smaller}
The US MNC index holds the 60 US multinationals with the highest share of
international revenue.
:::

::: notes
*[cuttable - 5.1 already tests the mechanics; this one tests judgement]*

Five minutes in pairs. There is no single number to compute, which is the point
- this one tests whether they can reason with the measures rather than apply
them.

*[ask]* Start with the easy observation. Which has the highest return?

The international funds, one fifty-eight against one seventeen. But by now they
should not stop there.

*[ask]* So divide by risk. Return per unit of standard deviation?

Funds, nought point two seven three. S&P, nought point two seven five. MNC
index, nought point three zero six. The funds' advantage in raw return almost
exactly disappears once you account for how much more they moved - and the MNC
index beats both.

*[point at the beta column]*

Now the interesting column. The funds have a beta of nought point six nine
against the US market, while both US portfolios sit at about one.

*[ask]* What does that tell you?

That the funds really did hold something different. They were genuinely less
exposed to US market movements - that is international diversification showing
up in the data.

*[pause]*

Then the conclusion worth writing down, and it has two halves.

The funds delivered real diversification, visible in the beta. But they did not
deliver better risk-adjusted performance than simply holding American
multinationals - firms that earn abroad and so carry foreign exposure inside a
domestic share.

*[ask]* So is buying an international fund worth the fees?

On this evidence, debatable. You can get part of the exposure at home. It is a
genuinely open question and a good one to leave with them.
:::

## 1 · Why almost nobody does it

:::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
**Home bias.** Investors hold far more domestic equity than any model
recommends. Four explanations are offered:

-   Domestic securities provide services foreign ones do not, such as
    **hedging domestic inflation**.
-   **Barriers**, formal and informal — legal, administrative, transaction and
    information costs, taxes.
-   The **prudent man rule**: institutions may simply be forbidden to hold more
    than a set fraction abroad.
-   It may be fading, as markets integrate and country funds and international
    mutual funds spread.
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
**Large-cap bias.** Portfolios that do go abroad concentrate in large firms —
and large firms are the worst vehicle for the job.

-   Large caps are typically **multinationals**, with foreign customers and
    investors, so their returns are driven by **common global factors** and are
    highly correlated.
-   **Small-cap** firms are driven by **local** factors, so they are the more
    effective instrument for international diversification.
:::
::::

::: notes
Close the session on the puzzle.

We have spent an hour establishing that international diversification improves
risk-adjusted performance in every country studied, and that it is easy and
cheap to obtain. So:

*[ask]* Why does the average investor hold ninety percent of their money at home?

Let them try before you give the list. The four explanations are on the slide
and none of them is fully convincing, which is worth admitting - home bias is
still an open puzzle in the literature.

Take the second and third seriously, because they are the testable ones.
Barriers are real but have fallen enormously, and home bias has not fallen
nearly as fast. The prudent man rule is real and binding for pension funds, but
it does not explain household behaviour.

*[right column]*

Then the second bias, which is subtler and a nice one to finish on.

Suppose you do invest abroad. You will almost certainly buy large, familiar,
listed companies - Toyota, Siemens, Nestlé.

*[ask]* What is wrong with that?

Those are exactly the firms whose returns are driven by the same global factors
as your own large caps. You have bought a foreign label on a correlated asset.

The firms that would actually diversify you are the small, locally oriented
ones you have never heard of - and those are the hardest to buy.

Leave them with that: the easiest foreign investment to make is the one that
diversifies you least.
:::
